section: Antibiotic Management of Suspected Sepsis in the NICU › Background, Flowchart: Antibiotic Management in NICU Suspected Bacterial Sepsis, Flowchart: Interpretation of Primary Blood Culture Results, Flowchart: Interpretation of Follow-up Blood Culture Results, Further Considerations

scope.population: Infants of any gestational age in the NICU with suspected bacterial sepsis, from birth through the NICU stay, at the Kaiser Permanente Riverside and Moreno Valley NICUs. The section splits them at 7 days of age; "beyond the newborn period" is read, as an assumption, as NICU infants evaluated after the first days of life, a group the literature studies mostly as very preterm or VLBW infants (the manual does not define the phrase, which can also mean after 28 days); "severely ill infants" is read as NICU infants in this group, a phrase no retrieved guideline defines.
scope.topic: Work-up, empiric and pathogen-directed antibiotic choice, and blood culture interpretation for suspected bacterial sepsis in NICU infants. The flowcharts are images and are not checkable; dosing Tables 1 and 2 are a separate item.
scope.basis: Section heading "Antibiotic Management of Suspected Sepsis in the NICU" and Background line 17: "Starting antibiotics for suspected bacterial sepsis is common in patients in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit."

claims.manual_text: Assessment for a urinary tract infection is indicated in most patients beyond the newborn period, as a high proportion of severe bacterial infections are caused by urinary tract infections.
claims.summary: A UK guideline advises against routine urine testing in late-onset evaluations in neonatal units [NICE2026], whereas NICU cohorts of very preterm or VLBW infants report UTI in 7% and 8.5% of infants and in 11.3% of tested evaluations and favor urine testing [Kilpatrick2024; Drumm2019; Mohseny2018], although the 7% likely includes some positive urine isolates misclassified as UTI [Kilpatrick2024], a low-birth-weight cohort reports a rate of 1.3% [Janardhan2024], and none of these gives UTI as a share of severe infection or a figure for term or older NICU infants.

evidence.quote: Do not routinely perform urine microscopy or culture as part of the investigations for early-onset neonatal infection, or late-onset neonatal infection for babies in neonatal units.
Of 86,492 included infants, 5,988 (7%) had a UTI.
Neonatal clinicians should consider obtaining urine culture in the setting of late-onset sepsis evaluations in VLBW infants.
UTI was diagnosed in 8.5% of VLBW infants (range 2-15.9%) and in 13.8% of infants weighing < 1000 g at birth.
Urine culture should be included in all LOS evaluations in order to facilitate accurate diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
In half of this group, urine analysis was performed identifying UTI in 11.3% (24/212).
Rate of UTIs among LBW neonates was 1.3% for the entire study period and typical uropathogens were the cause.

There is likely misclassification of some positive urine isolates as UTI, since additional diagnostic criteria for UTI, including biochemical urine studies (e.g., urinalysis), were not analyzed and colony counts were not available for analysis.

claims.manual_text: If a urinary tract infection is suspected obtain catheterized urinalysis with urine culture; bagged urines are not acceptable.
claims.summary: No retrieved source compares urine collection methods in NICU infants: the one NICU cohort with method data, in infants <32 weeks, used catheterization, suprapubic aspiration and bag collection and does not report contamination by method [Mohseny2018].

evidence.quote: Urine specimens were obtained by one of four methods: sterile urethral catheterization (SUC), suprapubic aspiration (SA), bag collection (BC), or collecting fresh urine from a catheter a demeure (CAD).
Bag collection | 56 | 5.3

claims.manual_text: If intubated or with a tracheostomy, consider a respiratory culture with gram-stain.
claims.summary: No guideline or trial was found, and the two single-unit observational neonatal studies retrieved do not recommend for or against culture: in a US level IV NICU positive tracheal aspirates were not associated with markers of infection but were associated with prolonged antibiotic exposure [Langston2020], and in an Indian unit positive aspirates in suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia were associated with longer respiratory support and a negative aspirate might encourage stopping antibiotics [Tuteja2022]; neither covers tracheostomy patients.

evidence.quote: Positive tracheal aspirates were not significantly associated with clinical, laboratory, or radiographic markers used in clinical practice to screen for infection.
Despite the lack of positive clinical associations, a positive tracheal aspirate culture was associated with increased risk of prolonged antibiotic exposure.
Positive ETA culture was associated with longer needs for respiratory supports. Negative ETA culture might encourage clinicians to stop antibiotics.

claims.manual_text: If wounds are present and appear infected, consider cultures of the wound and drainage of any abscess.
claims.summary: NICE advises against skin swabs without clinical signs of localised infection and advises a swab sample for clinical signs of umbilical infection [NICE2026], but it does not address wound culture or abscess drainage.

evidence.quote: Do not perform skin swab microscopy or culture as part of the investigations for neonatal infection if there are no clinical signs of a localised infection.
take a swab sample for microscopy and culture

claims.manual_text: For severely ill infants, meningitis should be considered, and CSF studies obtained as appropriate.
claims.summary: NICE advises lumbar puncture, if safe, when there is strong clinical suspicion of neonatal infection or signs of meningitis, after stabilising an unstable baby [NICE2026], and blood cultures were negative in one third of VLBW infants with meningitis and in 38% of those ≥34 weeks [Stoll2004; Garges2006]; the phrase "severely ill" is not used in these sources.

evidence.quote: If it is safe to do so, perform a lumbar puncture to obtain a cerebrospinal fluid sample when: • there is a strong clinical suspicion of neonatal infection or • there are clinical symptoms or signs suggesting meningitis.
Treat and stabilise any of the following before performing a lumbar puncture: • unprotected airway • respiratory compromise • shock • uncontrolled seizures • bleeding risk.
One third (45 of 134) of the infants with meningitis had negative BCs.
Only 57 (62%) of 92 patients had a concomitant-positive blood culture; 35 (38%) of 92 had a negative blood culture.

claims.manual_text: For infants < 30 days old herpes simplex virus (HSV) should be considered in severely ill infants. If HSV is suspected obtain HSV surface, blood, and CSF PCRs with ALT.
claims.summary: PCR is the test of choice for neonatal herpes [CDCSTI2021], published work-ups include surface, blood and CSF testing with ALT [Kimberlin2013], and critical illness and elevated ALT were more common with HSV [Dantuluri2025], but in infants presenting for sepsis evaluation outside the NICU the age windows named are ≤21 days [Dantuluri2025] and the first 14 days of life [Dungu2023].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests a narrower age window in sepsis evaluations: recent guidelines name infants ≤21 days with certain risk factors [Dantuluri2025], and in Danish emergency departments neonates whose HSV resembled invasive bacterial infection all presented within the first 14 days of life [Dungu2023]. 2013 guidance for exposed neonates advised surface PCR in addition to, not instead of, surface culture [Kimberlin2013].

evidence.quote: Recent guidelines recommend considering HSV in infants ≤21 days of age presenting for sepsis evaluations with certain risk factors.

Among infants presenting for neonatal sepsis evaluations, those without HSV infection are unlikely to present with seizures, skin lesions, elevated ALT, thrombocytopenia, CSF pleocytosis, or critical illness compared to infants with HSV.
Twenty presented with symptoms resembling IBI, all within the first 14 days of life.
PCR is also the test of choice for diagnosing HSV infections affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and systemic infections (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, and neonatal herpes).
The sensitivity of PCR assay on surface specimens has not been studied; if used, surface PCR assay should be performed in addition to (and not instead of) the gold-standard surface culture.
lumbar puncture with CSF sent for indices and HSV DNA PCR assay, in addition to serum alanine transaminase
PCR assay of blood has been added to the laboratory evaluation for neonatal HSV disease.

claims.manual_text: Cefepime and vancomycin provide broad coverage for gram-negative and gram-positive infection in NICU infants. Very few bacteria are not covered by this combination.
claims.summary: Isolate data show cefepime nonsusceptibility of 3.2% (15 of 465) and 6.5% (3 of 46) in neonatal E. coli [FlanneryEcoli2021; Flannery2022s], 9.9% nonsusceptibility of NICU gram-negative bacilli to third-generation cephalosporins or cefepime pooled [Patel2017] and no vancomycin nonsusceptibility among tested early-onset gram-positive isolates, which were few (for example S. aureus 3, CoNS 2, Enterococcus 13), while covering all 239 early-onset isolates would have taken vancomycin, a carbapenem and an antifungal added to ampicillin and gentamicin [Flannery2022s]; these are in-vitro data for each drug, with no trial of the pair and no matching late-onset gram-positive series.

evidence.quote: Among cephalosporins, 11/51 (21.6%), 3/56 (5.4%) and 3/46 (6.5%) E. coli isolates were non-susceptible to cefazolin, ceftriaxone or cefepime, respectively.
Third-generation cephalosporin agents or cefepimed 10/94 (10.6) 5/73 (6.8) 6/41 (14.6) 1/14 (7.1) 22/222 (9.9)
evidence.location: Table 2 (used because the abstract prints different percentages, for example third-generation cephalosporin 7.0% against 9.9% here, and 214 isolates against 230 in the Results and Table 2; cefepime is pooled with third-generation agents)

evidence.quote: S. aureus isolates tested were susceptible to vancomycin and variably susceptible to penicillin and gentamicin.
but only the addition of vancomycin, a carbapenem, and an antifungal agent together with ampicillin and gentamicin would provide adequate empiric antibiotic coverage for all 239 isolates.

claims.manual_text: Of note: HSV infections and Candida should be considered for severe infections, and, if suspected, started on treatment while the workup is under way.
claims.summary: CDC advises prompt systemic acyclovir for neonatal herpes and gives a regimen for known or suspected disease [CDCSTI2021], and a neonatal review and a cohort from all neonatal and paediatric emergency departments in Denmark favor a targeted rather than universal approach to acyclovir [Dantuluri2024; Dungu2023]; for Candida the guideline's neonatal section gives treatment but no empiric recommendation [Pappas2016].

evidence.quote: All newborn infants who have neonatal herpes should be promptly evaluated and treated with systemic acyclovir.

The recommended regimen for infants treated for known or suspected neonatal herpes is acyclovir 20 mg/kg body weight IV every 8 hours for 14 days if disease is limited to the skin and mucous membranes, or for 21 days for disseminated disease and disease involving the CNS.
The literature supports a targeted approach to evaluation and empiric acyclovir treatment for neonatal HSV, but additional studies are needed to validate this approach given the rarity of disease.
Therefore, we propose not to treat all neonates suspected of IBI with empiric acyclovir, as current European guidelines suggest.
AmB deoxycholate, 1 mg/kg daily, is recommended for neonates with disseminated candidiasis (strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence).
All neonatal and paediatric emergency departments in Denmark from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2019.

claims.manual_text: Dosing medications for meningitis should be considered in severely ill patients unless meningitis has been ruled out.
claims.summary: No retrieved source tests meningitic against standard dosing before meningitis is excluded: NICE addresses drug choice for suspected meningitis in neonatal units [NICE2026] and a review reports that cefepime dosing references for neonates vary [McDonald2021].

evidence.quote: If a baby is in a neonatal unit and meningitis is suspected but the causative pathogen is unknown (for example, because the cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain is uninformative), treat with intravenous amoxicillin and cefotaxime.
Recommended cefepime dosing strategies in neonates varies in commonly utilized dosing references with regard to dose and frequency.

claims.manual_text: Cefepime provides broader coverage of gram-negative rods when compared to gentamicin, as well as providing coverage for MSSA, and resistant Streptococci.
claims.summary: Only the gram-negative limb has tested evidence, in vitro: nonsusceptibility of NICU isolates was 14.8% to gentamicin and 9.9% to third-generation cephalosporins or cefepime pooled, so cefepime alone is not reported, in Table 2 figures that differ from the abstract's [Patel2017], and in neonatal E. coli it was 15.2% to gentamicin and 3.2% to cefepime [FlanneryEcoli2021] or 10.0% (8 of 80) and 6.5% (3 of 46) in early-onset isolates [Flannery2022s]; MSSA coverage appears only in a Methods definition of adequate therapy that also counts aminoglycosides [Thaden2015], with no S. aureus cefepime result in Table 1b, and for resistant streptococci early-onset viridans streptococci were nonsusceptible to penicillin in 3 of 6 and to cefepime in 0 of 2, not cross-tabulated [Flannery2022s].

Adequate empirical antibiotics for MSSA included all aminoglycosides, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins (with the exception of ceftazidime), penicillins combined with beta-lactamase inhibitors, nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin, methicillin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, and rifampin.

23% of 214 GNB isolates were nonsusceptible to antimicrobial agents, including gentamicin (14.8%), piperacillin-tazobactam (9.9%), third-generation cephalosporin (7.0%), and/or carbapenem agents (4.5%).

claims.manual_text: Ampicillin provides coverage for Listeria, Enterococci, and most Streptococci.
claims.summary: All GBS, group A streptococcal and Enterococcus isolates tested in early-onset sepsis, and 3 of 6 viridans streptococci, were susceptible to ampicillin and/or penicillin, with ampicillin nonsusceptibility in 0 of 48 GBS, 0 of 14 Enterococcus and 0 of 1 Listeria [Flannery2022s], and for neonatal listeriosis a review names ampicillin or amoxicillin as treatment of choice [Koopmans2023] and NICE lists amoxicillin with gentamicin [NICE2026]; matching late-onset susceptibility data were not retrieved.

evidence.quote: All GBS, Group A Streptococcus, Enterococci spp. and 3/6 viridans Streptococci isolates tested were susceptible to ampicillin and/or penicillin (Table 1).
In neonates with listeriosis in the first week of life, ampicillin or amoxicillin (100-300 mg/kg/day during 14 days, parenterally) is the antimicrobial treatment of choice.
If the blood culture or cerebrospinal fluid culture is positive for listeria, consider stopping cefotaxime and treating with amoxicillin and gentamicin.

claims.manual_text: MSSA, gram-negative rods, and Streptococci make up the majority of concerning infections in NICU infants older than 7 days.
claims.summary: In very preterm infants with onset after 3 days, S. aureus (23.0%), gram-negative bacteria (32.0%) and GBS (4.7%) together made up 59.7% of isolates and CoNS 29.3% [Flannery2022], gram-negative organisms were 33.3% of pathogens after 72 hours in a two-system NICU cohort [Mukhopadhyay2022], and MSSA was 72% of S. aureus in US NICUs [Ericson2015a]; these series use a 3-day cut-off, not 7 days, and Flannery did not separate MSSA.

evidence.quote: Gram-positive bacteria accounted for 62.9% of isolates and gram-negatives accounted for 32.0% (Table 3).
CONS (3549 of 12 117; 29.3%) and Staphylococcus aureus (2784 of 12117; 23.0%) were the most-common pathogens.
For Staphylococcus aureus, data collection did not distinguish between methicillin- sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) isolates.
Gram-negative organisms were second most common (33.3%), followed by fungi (6.1%) and polymicrobial infections (2.6%) (Table 1).
Infections were caused more commonly by MSSA (2868/3978, 72%) than MRSA (1110/3978, 28%).

claims.manual_text: Risk of Staphylococcal infection is independent of if a central line is present.
claims.summary: The line is read as S. aureus only, although the manual says "Staphylococcal", because no evidence given addresses CoNS: in a US NICU cohort a central line was in place for 40.3% of late-onset invasive S. aureus infections, but 87.5% of infected infants had a line during their stay against 22.0% of uninfected infants, unadjusted [Jennings2025], intravascular catheters are cited as a risk factor for S. aureus bloodstream infection [Thaden2015], and a NICU white paper says colonization predisposes to invasive infection and that S. aureus remains a frequent device-associated infection, without comparing infants by line status [Akinboyo2020]; no retrieved study gives an adjusted estimate.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests S. aureus infection is not confined to infants with a central line: a line was in place for 40.3% of late-onset invasive infections in a US cohort [Jennings2025]. Independence is not shown, because 87.5% of infected infants had a line during their stay against 22.0% of uninfected infants in unadjusted data [Jennings2025], and intravascular catheters are cited as a risk factor [Thaden2015].

evidence.quote: There was a total of 1762 events (Figure 2), most of which included bloodstream infections (BSIs) (1505 events [85.4%]) (eTable 1 in Supplement 1), and 710 infections (40.3%) occurred while a central line was in place.
Central line placed during stay 1509 (87.5) 102 821 (22.0) 1.75
Several risk factors for S. aureus BSI have been identified, including intravascular catheters
Neonates may acquire S. aureus as part of their normal developing microbiota; yet, colonization predisposes to invasive infection.
evidence.location: Introduction (white paper; S. aureus here means MRSA and MSSA)

evidence.quote: Despite decreasing device utilization rates within the NICU, S. aureus remains a frequent cause of healthcare-associated and device-associated infections.

claims.manual_text: Gram-negative rods, Streptococci, and Enterococci make up most infections in NICU infants 7 days and younger.
claims.summary: In US surveillance of onset within 72 hours, Table 1 lists 107 of 235 cases as gram-negative, 70 as GBS, 30 as other streptococci and 13 as Enterococcus [Stoll2020], and E. coli and GBS were also the leading pathogens in very preterm infants with onset in the first 3 days [Flannery2021]; days 4 to 7 are not reported separately and fall within late-onset series, where CoNS (29.3%) and S. aureus (23.0%) were the most common pathogens in very preterm infants [Flannery2022].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests this organism mix holds for onset within 72 hours of birth [Stoll2020] or, in very preterm infants, the first 3 days [Flannery2021]; published series place days 4 to 7 with late-onset sepsis, where CoNS and S. aureus were the most common pathogens in very preterm infants [Flannery2022].

evidence.quote: Gram-positive organisms were identified in 120 of 235 infants; gram-negative organisms, in 107; and fungal organisms and polymicrobial infections, in 4 each (Table 1).

Escherichia coli (538 of 1158; 46.5%) and group B Streptococcus (218 of 1158; 18.8%) were the most common pathogens.
Early-onset sepsis defined by isolation of pathogenic species from blood or cerebrospinal fluid culture within 72 hours of birth and antibiotic treatment for at least 5 days or until death.
EOS was defined as a culture-confirmed infection of the blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by a prespecified bacterial pathogen (Supplemental Information) in the first 3 days after birth.
Late-onset sepsis was defined as isolation of a pathogenic bacteria from blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid, or fungi from blood, obtained >3 days after birth.
The most common pathogens were coagulase negative staphylococci (29.3%) and Staphylococcus aureus (23.0%), but 34 different pathogens were identified.

claims.manual_text: Based on data from >22,000 blood cultures sent for KP SoCal NICU patients, >93% of likely pathogens will grow from blood cultures by 36 hours, and the likelihood of a positive culture resulting after 36 hours is 0.12%.
claims.summary: In a Kaiser Permanente Northern California and Pennsylvania Hospital cohort of cultures obtained >72 hours after birth, 93.5% of non-CoNS cultures were positive by 36 hours and the chance of later growth was 0.5% for non-CoNS organisms, or 1.8% with CoNS managed as pathogens [Mukhopadhyay2022]; in a separate 19-hospital early-onset study 94% were positive by 36 hours [Kuzniewicz2020], 91.2% of all positive cultures in one level IV NICU and 100% of definite and possible pathogens in another were positive by then [Nishihara2024; Hurst2026], NICE sets decision points of 36 hours for early-onset and 48 hours for late-onset infection, each with conditions [NICE2026], and the manual's local dataset was not found in print.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests a higher chance of growth after 36 hours in late-onset evaluations (cultures >72 hours after birth): a culture negative at 36 hours later grew a non-CoNS pathogen with a probability of 0.5%, and 1.8% when CoNS managed as pathogens are included [Mukhopadhyay2022]. These figures come from a formula that uses culture positivity, so they may differ elsewhere [Mukhopadhyay2022]. NICE uses 36 hours for early-onset and 48 hours for late-onset infection, each with conditions, because late-onset cultures can take longer to turn positive [NICE2026].

evidence.quote: Excluding coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), 275/294 (93.5%) cultures were flagged positive by 36 hours.
The probability of detecting a bacterial pathogen after 36 hours was 1.8% (95% CI 1.4–2.2) and the probability of detecting a non-CoNS pathogen after 36 hours was 0.5% (95% CI 0.3–0.7).
We found a low probability (1.8%) for a culture that is negative at 36 hours to signal growth thereafter, and an even lower probability (0.5%) that it will detect a non-CoNS organism.
We determined the probability of a culture growing a bacterial pathogen after 36 hours using the formula provided by Lambregts et al
evidence.location: Methods, Analysis (the quote stops before the formula, which the source sets as a fraction: P = [(1−TTPe)*X] / [1−(TTPe*X)] * 100)

evidence.quote: where TTPe is the proportion of positive blood cultures growing ≤36 hours after birth, and X is the rate of positivity for blood cultures obtained >72 hours after birth.
evidence.location: Methods, Analysis (defines the terms of the formula; the e in TTPe is a subscript in the source)

evidence.quote: Blood cultures were identified as positive by 24 hours after they were obtained in 68% of cases; by 36 hours in 94% of cases; and by 48 hours in 97% of cases.
Median TTP [IQR] was 21.1 [14.3, 25.2] hours, with 91.2% positive at 36 h, and 96.1% positive at 48 h.
At 24 hours, 97% (30/31) of definite pathogens were reported as positive, and at 36 hours, 100% (52/52) of definite and possible pathogens were reported as positive.
Infants with positive blood cultures obtained >72 hours after birth.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) were classified as pathogens when managed accordingly by the clinical team with ≥5 days of antibiotics.

Observational study of blood cultures growing pathogenic species obtained within 72 hours of birth from infants born at 23-42 weeks gestation, at 19 hospitals in Northern California, Boston, and Philadelphia.

For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring.

For babies given antibiotics because of suspected late-onset infection, consider stopping the antibiotics at 48 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection and • the levels and trends of C‑reactive protein concentration are reassuring.

This means that it can take longer for a blood culture to become positive for late-onset than early-onset infection and so treatment needs to continue for longer until a negative blood culture result can be confirmed.
evidence.location: Rationale, decisions 48 hours after starting antibiotics for late-onset neonatal infection

claims.manual_text: Treating a patient for culture negative sepsis with 5 days of antibiotic may be reasonable in select patients where infection is highly suspected, but appropriately drawn cultures were negative.
claims.summary: The sources differ on this case: for early-onset disease with a negative culture and strongly suspected sepsis NICE says 7 days, for late-onset disease it says shorter than 7 days but only with prompt recovery, with daily review if antibiotics continue past 48 hours despite a negative culture [NICE2026], and in a randomized trial in neonates ≥35 weeks with culture-negative early-onset sepsis individualised treatment (median 3 days) was non-inferior to a standard 5-7 days [Carlsen2026]; in ELBW infants with sterile cultures the median initial empirical course was 5 days and courses of ≥5 days were associated with necrotizing enterocolitis or death [Cotten2009].

evidence.quote: Give intravenous antibiotic treatment for a total of 7 days for babies with a positive blood culture or negative blood culture if sepsis has been strongly suspected.

Use a shorter treatment duration than 7 days when the baby makes a prompt recovery, and either no pathogen is identified or the pathogen identified is a common commensal (for example, coagulase negative staphylococcus).
If continuing antibiotics for longer than 48 hours for suspected late‑onset neonatal infection despite negative blood culture, review the baby at least once every 24 hours.

In neonates with probable EOS, a clinically guided, individualised treatment strategy was non-inferior to standard therapy with respect to infection-related readmission and reduced treatment duration to a median of 3 days.
Standard treatment was 5-7 days.
The median therapy duration was 5 days (range: 1–36 days); 2147 infants (53%) received prolonged empirical therapy
We defined prolonged initial empirical antibiotic treatment as ≥5 days of initial empirical antibiotic treatment with sterile culture results.
Prolonged initial empirical antibiotic therapy may be associated with increased risk of necrotizing entero-colitis or death and should be used with caution.

claims.manual_text: CSF testing should be considered for all severely ill infants, those with gram-negative bacteremia, group B strep bacteremia, candidemia, or with concern for HSV.
claims.summary: NICE advises considering lumbar puncture, if safe, in a baby on antibiotics with no lumbar puncture at presentation who has a positive blood culture other than CoNS, which covers gram-negative and GBS bacteremia through a general positive-culture trigger, and performing it, if safe, for strong clinical suspicion of neonatal infection [NICE2026], the IDSA guideline recommends it in neonates with Candida in blood or urine [Pappas2016], CSF PCR is the method of choice for CNS HSV [Kimberlin2013], GBS and E. coli were the commonest meningitis pathogens in a level IV NICU [OHearn2024], and 11% of Serratia bloodstream isolates had a concordant CSF culture across NICUs [Beam2014]; no organism-specific AAP text could be read.

evidence.quote: If it is safe to do so, perform a lumbar puncture to obtain a cerebrospinal fluid sample when: • there is a strong clinical suspicion of neonatal infection or • there are clinical symptoms or signs suggesting meningitis.

Consider performing a lumbar puncture to obtain a cerebrospinal fluid sample in a baby who did not have a lumbar puncture at presentation who is receiving antibiotics, if it is thought safe to do so and if: • the baby has a positive blood culture (other than coagulase negative staphylococcus) or • the baby does not respond satisfactorily to antibiotic treatment, or • there is a strong clinical suspicion of infection or • there are clinical symptoms or signs suggesting meningitis.
A lumbar puncture and a dilated retinal examination are recommended in neonates with cultures positive for Candida species from blood and/or urine (strong recommendation; low-quality evidence).
PCR assay is now the method of choice for documenting CNS involvement in an infant suspected of having HSV disease.

Group B streptococcus (GBS) and Escherichia coli (E coli) were most common pathogens, however, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) predominated among infants with NS devices.
Serratia marcescens (24/227, 11%) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (7/64, 11%) had the highest proportion of concordant blood-CSF culture pairs.

claims.manual_text: Coagulase negative Staphylococci typically do not cause CNS infection except if there is hardware in the CNS or through direct inoculation via CNS injury.
claims.summary: In a quaternary NICU 12 of 14 infants with CoNS meningitis had a neurosurgical device and the other 2 had concomitant bacteremia [OHearn2024], across NICUs only 4 of 1265 CoNS-positive blood cultures had a paired CSF culture positive for CoNS [Beam2014], and NICE excepts CoNS from its positive-blood-culture trigger for lumbar puncture, without giving a reason in the recommendation [NICE2026]; direct inoculation is not addressed.

evidence.quote: Among the infants with CoNS meningitis (12 isolates of Staphylococcus epidermidis, 1 S warneri, and 1 S haemolyticus), 12 of 14 had a NS device at the time of diagnosis.
The 2 infants without NS devices had concomitant bacteremia and were adjudicated as pathogenic in conjunction with pediatric infectious diseases consultants.
CoNS represented 1265/9408 (13%) of the total blood-CSF culture pair population, but only 4/1265 (<1%) of the paired CSF cultures were positive for CoNS.

Consider performing a lumbar puncture to obtain a cerebrospinal fluid sample in a baby who did not have a lumbar puncture at presentation who is receiving antibiotics, if it is thought safe to do so and if: • the baby has a positive blood culture (other than coagulase negative staphylococcus) or • the baby does not respond satisfactorily to antibiotic treatment, or • there is a strong clinical suspicion of infection or • there are clinical symptoms or signs suggesting meningitis.

claims.manual_text: Atypical organisms may require specific treatment and diagnostics. These include Candida and other fungal infections and HSV.
claims.summary: Neonatal Candida has its own recommendations, including lumbar puncture, dilated retinal examination and amphotericin B deoxycholate [Pappas2016], and neonatal HSV has PCR testing and acyclovir regimens [CDCSTI2021]; other fungal infections are not addressed in these lines.

evidence.quote: A lumbar puncture and a dilated retinal examination are recommended in neonates with cultures positive for Candida species from blood and/or urine (strong recommendation; low-quality evidence).
AmB deoxycholate, 1 mg/kg daily, is recommended for neonates with disseminated candidiasis (strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence).
PCR is also the test of choice for diagnosing HSV infections affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and systemic infections (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, and neonatal herpes).

The recommended regimen for infants treated for known or suspected neonatal herpes is acyclovir 20 mg/kg body weight IV every 8 hours for 14 days if disease is limited to the skin and mucous membranes, or for 21 days for disseminated disease and disease involving the CNS.

claims.manual_text: There is no benefit in using broader spectrum antibiotics once a pathogen is isolated, and in some cases broader spectrum antibiotics may lead to worse outcomes.
claims.summary: No retrieved neonatal study examines broader against narrower therapy after a pathogen is isolated; the harm data come from other settings, where broad-spectrum exposure was associated with invasive fungal infection [Esaiassen2017] and ampicillin with cefotaxime in the first 3 days with more deaths than ampicillin with gentamicin [Clark2006].

evidence.quote: Prolonged antibiotic exposure in uninfected preterm infants is associated with an increased risk of NEC and/or death, and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure is associated with an increased risk of IFI.

Logistic modeling showed that neonates treated with ampicillin/cefotaxime were more likely to die (adjusted odds ratio: 1.5; 95% confidence interval: 1.4-1.7) and were less likely to be discharged to home or foster care than were neonates treated with ampicillin/gentamicin.

claims.manual_text: Typically, the narrowest spectrum beta lactam is the preferred treatment.
claims.summary: For neonates NICE lists changing to benzylpenicillin for GBS meningitis and to amoxicillin for listeria, each with gentamicin [NICE2026], and a review names ampicillin or amoxicillin as treatment of choice in neonatal listeriosis [Koopmans2023]; these are organism-specific, and no general neonatal statement was retrieved.

evidence.quote: If the cerebrospinal fluid culture is positive for group B streptococcus, consider changing the antibiotic treatment to: • benzylpenicillin sodium 50 mg/kg every 12 hours, normally for at least 14 days
If the blood culture or cerebrospinal fluid culture is positive for listeria, consider stopping cefotaxime and treating with amoxicillin and gentamicin.
In neonates with listeriosis in the first week of life, ampicillin or amoxicillin (100-300 mg/kg/day during 14 days, parenterally) is the antimicrobial treatment of choice.

claims.manual_text: The addition of vancomycin is sufficient coverage for most gram-positive infections, as nearly all Streptococci and coagulase negative Staphylococcus are vancomycin sensitive. Vancomycin can be substituted in place of ampicillin while final sensitivities and speciation are pending for these organisms. For instance changing a combination of ampicillin and cefepime to vancomycin plus cefepime is typically sufficient.
claims.summary: Only the susceptibility clause has tested evidence, and it is small and all from isolates within 72 hours of birth: none of 32 GBS, 6 viridans streptococci, 2 group A streptococci, 2 other Streptococcus spp., 4 S. bovis, 3 S. pneumoniae, 13 Enterococcus or 2 CoNS was nonsusceptible to vancomycin [Flannery2022s], and a background sentence describes CoNS bloodstream infection as most reliably treated with vancomycin [Ericson2015b]; susceptibility tests a drug and organism pair, and no retrieved source tests substituting vancomycin for ampicillin while speciation is pending or shows that change is typically sufficient.

evidence.quote: Reassuringly, GBS isolates tested were susceptible to ampicillin, penicillin, vancomycin, and cephalosporins.
CoNS BSI is most reliably treated with vancomycin; however, concerns about side effects and promoting resistance often delay empirical vancomycin therapy until culture results become available.

EOS was defined as isolation of a pathogen from blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture obtained within 72 hours of birth and treatment with antibiotics for 5 or more days (or <5 days if death occurred while receiving antibiotic therapy).

claims.manual_text: For Listeria and Enterococci infections ampicillin should be continued.
claims.summary: For neonatal listeriosis a review names ampicillin or amoxicillin, which can be combined with gentamicin, as treatment of choice [Koopmans2023] and NICE lists amoxicillin with gentamicin [NICE2026]; neither addresses Enterococcus therapy in neonates.

evidence.quote: In neonates with listeriosis in the first week of life, ampicillin or amoxicillin (100-300 mg/kg/day during 14 days, parenterally) is the antimicrobial treatment of choice.
Both regimens can be prescribed in combination with gentamicin (2 mg/kg during 7 days) (496).
If the blood culture or cerebrospinal fluid culture is positive for listeria, consider stopping cefotaxime and treating with amoxicillin and gentamicin.

claims.manual_text: S. aureus is difficult to treat and often leads to severe and complicated infections, so antibiotics should be optimized quickly after diagnosis.
claims.summary: Late-onset invasive S. aureus infection carried an absolute mortality difference of 5.3% [Jennings2025] and mortality was 26% with MRSA and 24% with MSSA in VLBW infants [Shane2012], and inadequate empirical therapy was associated with higher 30-day mortality in MRSA but not MSSA bloodstream infection, without a mortality increase from short treatment delays, an analysis the authors call limited by low numbers [Thaden2015].

evidence.quote: Compared with matched infants without a late-onset invasive S aureus infection, infected infants had an absolute difference in mortality rate of 5.3% (95% CI, 3.8%-6.8%).
Mortality was high with both MRSA (23 of 88, 26%) and MSSA (55 of 228, 24%).

Inadequate empirical antibiotic therapy was associated with increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio: 2.03; 95% confidence interval: 1.08-3.82) among infants with MRSA BSI. Inadequate empirical antibiotic therapy was not associated with increases in mortality among infants with MSSA BSI.
Among infants with MSSA BSI who received either vancomycin or a beta-lactam therapy, no increase in 30-day mortality was observed if therapy was delayed 1 day
Among infants with MRSA BSI, delays in vancomycin therapy of 1, 2, or 3 days were not associated with increased mortality.
However, this temporal analysis was limited by the low number of infants with MRSA BSI who received vancomycin therapy with 2- and 3-day delays.

claims.manual_text: Cefepime and oxacillin have excellent activity against MSSA and are appropriate while final cultures are pending. Vancomycin has activity against S. aureus, but less so than oxacillin or cefepime for susceptible isolates.
claims.summary: No retrieved neonatal source compares cefepime, oxacillin and vancomycin for MSSA: in US NICUs no clear effect of early adequate therapy on mortality was seen in MSSA bloodstream infection regardless of drug class [Thaden2015], and in 97 neonates with suspected late-onset sepsis empiric nafcillin did not increase clinical worsening compared with vancomycin [Hanson2025].

evidence.quote: In infants with MSSA BSI, no clear effect of early adequate empirical antibiotic therapy on mortality was observed, regardless of the therapeutic drug class.
Use of nafcillin as the Gram-positive empiric treatment agent did not result in increased clinical worsening compared to vancomycin at our institution.
The final cohort included 97 neonates (46 VANC, 51 NAF).

claims.manual_text: MRSA infections are rare in the NICU outside of outbreak settings.
claims.summary: MSSA far exceeds MRSA in the NICU [CDC2020] and 1% of VLBW infants had MRSA [Shane2012], but MRSA made up 28% of S. aureus infections in two US cohorts and 22% in 2012 [Ericson2015a; Shane2012; Thaden2015], varied widely by site [Ericson2015a], and showed no evidence of outbreaks in one network [Shane2012]; later national data pooled MRSA and MSSA [Jennings2025], and a NICU white paper says most literature on preventing S. aureus (MRSA and MSSA) comes from outbreak control, with few data from endemic settings [Akinboyo2020].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests MRSA is less common than MSSA but is not limited to outbreaks: it caused 28% of invasive S. aureus infections across US NICUs from 1997 to 2012, with a site median of 26.3% [Ericson2015a], and a network cohort of VLBW infants born 2006 to 2008 found no evidence of temporal clustering or outbreaks [Shane2012]. Later national data pooled MRSA and MSSA [Jennings2025].

evidence.quote: Infections were caused more commonly by MSSA (2868/3978, 72%) than MRSA (1110/3978, 28%).
For the 100 sites with ≥10 episodes of invasive S. aureus infection, the proportion of invasive S. aureus infections caused by MRSA varied widely by site (median 26.3% [16.7, 36.8]).
Eighty-eight had MRSA (1% of all infants, 28% of infants with SA); 228 had MSSA (2.7% of all infants, 72% of infants with SA).
There was no evidence of temporal clustering or outbreaks of MRSA infections.
The proportion of BSIs caused by MRSA increased from 1997 (3/17, 18%) to 2006 (105/287, 37%) and decreased through 2012 (49/223, 22%)
While MRSA remains epidemiologically significant and a priority pathogen, MSSA infections far exceed MRSA infections in the NICU, so prevention strategies for S. aureus as a whole are needed.
Methicillin-resistant and methicillin-sensitive S aureus classification was not universally available; thus, all invasive S aureus infections were pooled.
Most available literature report on S. aureus prevention in the context of outbreak control; few data exist on this topic in endemic NICU settings.
evidence.location: Introduction (white paper; S. aureus here means MRSA and MSSA)

claims.manual_text: In non-improving patients with S. aureus infections vancomycin should be added in addition to oxacillin or cefepime until MRSA has been ruled out.
claims.summary: No retrieved neonatal source tests adding vancomycin according to clinical response: in NICU infants inadequate empirical therapy was associated with higher 30-day mortality in MRSA bloodstream infection, while delays in vancomycin of 1, 2 or 3 days were not associated with higher mortality [Thaden2015].

evidence.quote: Inadequate empirical antibiotic therapy was associated with increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio: 2.03; 95% confidence interval: 1.08-3.82) among infants with MRSA BSI.
Among infants with MRSA BSI, delays in vancomycin therapy of 1, 2, or 3 days were not associated with increased mortality.

claims.manual_text: This would typically involve broadening from gentamicin to cefepime. In severely ill children who are clinically worsening, broadening from cefepime to meropenem would be a consideration in discussion with Pediatric Infectious Diseases.
claims.summary: No retrieved guideline, trial or protocol addresses either step: NeoMero-1, a trial of empiric meropenem against standard care in neonatal late-onset sepsis, found no overall superiority of meropenem and did not test escalation from cefepime or worsening infants, and reserving meropenem for seriously ill premature neonates with suspected or proven gram-negative infection, worded in the abstract as neonates more likely to have gram-negative infection, is an author recommendation [Lutsar2020], while third-generation cephalosporins and cefepime being used more commonly as targeted gram-negative therapy in US NICUs describes what was prescribed [Patel2017].

evidence.quote: Within this study population, we found no evidence that meropenem was superior to SOC in terms of success at TOC, short term hearing disturbances, safety or mortality were similar in both treatment arms but the study was underpowered to detect the planned effect.

We recommend that meropenem should be reserved for seriously ill premature neonates with suspected or proven Gram-negative LOS, especially in NICUs in which microorganisms producing ESBL and AmpC beta-lactamases are circulating.
However, third-generation cephalosporin agents and cefepime were used more commonly as targeted therapy for identified Gram-negative pathogens.

We suggest that meropenem as broad-spectrum antibiotic should be reserved for neonates who are more likely to have Gram-negative LOS, especially in NICUs where microorganisms producing extended spectrum- and AmpC type beta-lactamases are circulating.

claims.manual_text: Meropenem escalation is not needed in patients with GNR infections who are stable or improving.
claims.summary: No retrieved study covers stable or improving infants with gram-negative infection: in NeoMero-1 success in gram-negative sepsis was 34% with meropenem and 23% with standard care, not statistically significant, and 27% and 13% in all culture-positive infants [Lutsar2020], and broad-spectrum exposure, in particular third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems, was linked to invasive fungal infection [Esaiassen2017].

evidence.quote: The success rate in Gram positive sepsis was 21% in meropenem vs 7% in SOC arm and in Gram negative sepsis 34% vs 23%, respectively; these differences were not statistically significant.
The respective numbers in patients with positive cultures were 17/63 (27%) vs. 10/77 (13%) (p = 0.022).

Eleven of 15 studies with data on broad- versus narrow-spectrum regimens reported an increased risk of IFI after broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, in particular with third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems.

claims.manual_text: The gram-negative coverage of antibiotics in the NICU is as follows: gentamicin 84%, cefepime 96%, meropenem 99%.
claims.summary: These figures could not be traced to a publication; other units report nonsusceptibility of gram-negative bacilli of 14.8% to gentamicin (0% to 21.5% by site), 9.9% to third-generation cephalosporins or cefepime pooled and 0.5% to carbapenems, in Table 2 figures that differ from the abstract's [Patel2017], 3.2% to cefepime in E. coli [FlanneryEcoli2021], and carbapenem resistance in <1% in Canada [Balay2025].

evidence.location: Table 2 (used because the abstract prints different percentages and 214 isolates against 230 in the Results and Table 2)

evidence.quote: Third-generation cephalosporin agents or cefepimed 10/94 (10.6) 5/73 (6.8) 6/41 (14.6) 1/14 (7.1) 22/222 (9.9)
evidence.location: Table 2 (used because the abstract prints different percentages, for example third-generation cephalosporin 7.0% against 9.9% here, and 214 isolates against 230 in the Results and Table 2; cefepime is pooled with third-generation agents)
Table 2 (the abstract prints 4.5%; the Results say less than 1%)

evidence.quote: Nonsusceptibility to gentamicin was most common, and the rates varied among the sites (0%–21.5%; P = .04).
The resistance to carbapenems was identified in <1% of the isolates.

claims.manual_text: Neonates are at high risk of contaminated blood cultures given the difficulty obtaining blood samples.
claims.summary: Contaminants were 13.4% of positive late-onset cultures in a two-system NICU cohort [Mukhopadhyay2022], 54 of 289 infants with organisms isolated in early-onset surveillance [Stoll2020] and 71% of CoNS-positive cases in one unit [CarbonellSahuquillo2025], but these sources do not compare the risk with other patients or link it to sampling difficulty.

evidence.quote: After excluding cultures that were repeat positive due to persistent bacteremia/fungemia (n=441, 40.8%) and contaminants (n=145, 13.4%), there were 496 unique episodes of late-onset bacteremia or fungemia in 447 infants.
During the 2-year study period, 289 infants among 217 480 live births had organisms isolated from blood and CSF. The organisms isolated from 54 infants were determined to be contaminants
Patients were subdivided into sepsis (29%) and probable contamination (71%).

claims.manual_text: Contaminants typically include skin or gut flora, such as coagulase negative Staphylococcus species (S. epidermidis, S. capitis, S. haemolyticus, S. hominis, S. warneri), low pathogenicity streptococci species, Aerococcus, Coryneforms, Micrococcus, etc.
claims.summary: NICE and NHSN name CoNS as a common commensal [NICE2026; NHSN2026], 71% of CoNS-positive cases in one unit were probable contamination [CarbonellSahuquillo2025], and cohort definitions class diphtheroids and Micrococcus as contaminants [Mukhopadhyay2022; Beam2014], although CoNS were also 29.3% of late-onset pathogens in very preterm infants when criteria for true infection were met [Flannery2022]; Aerococcus is not addressed in these sources.

evidence.quote: Use a shorter treatment duration than 7 days when the baby makes a prompt recovery, and either no pathogen is identified or the pathogen identified is a common commensal (for example, coagulase negative staphylococcus).
2 matching common commensals (such as coagulase-negative staphylococci)
Patients were subdivided into sepsis (29%) and probable contamination (71%).
Known commensal organisms such as diphtheroids, Micrococcus species, etc. were classified as contaminants.

We excluded blood cultures positive for organisms considered contaminants, including non-speciated streptococci, Bacillus sp., Corynebacterium sp., diphtheroids sp., Gram-positive rods (not including Listeria sp.), Lactobacillus sp., Micrococcus sp., Stomatococcus sp., and Bacteroides sp.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CONS) from blood or cerebrospinal fluid culture was considered a true case of late-onset sepsis if there were signs of generalized infection and ≥5 days of antibiotics.
CONS (3549 of 12 117; 29.3%) and Staphylococcus aureus (2784 of 12117; 23.0%) were the most-common pathogens.

claims.manual_text: Contamination is likely if repeated blood cultures are negative while not on an antibiotic that covers the organisms, or polymicrobial culture results.
claims.summary: A surveillance definition addresses single-specimen commensals, treating one in a single blood specimen as a contaminant [NHSN2026], and the manual's repeat-culture test is unstudied in these sources; polymicrobial episodes, including organisms from different specimens in one episode, made up 14% of bloodstream infection episodes in one NICU, a share counted after single-culture commensals were excluded, with more than 3-fold higher mortality [Pammi2014], and polymicrobial infections were counted among true episodes in a two-system cohort [Mukhopadhyay2022], but no source reports how often a polymicrobial culture is contaminated.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests polymicrobial growth in the NICU can represent true infection: after single-culture commensals were excluded, 14% of bloodstream infection episodes at one US NICU were polymicrobial, with more than 3-fold higher mortality [Pammi2014], and a two-system cohort counted polymicrobial infections among true episodes [Mukhopadhyay2022]. These figures do not show how often a polymicrobial culture is contaminated [Pammi2014; Mukhopadhyay2022].

evidence.quote: A common commensal identified in a single blood specimen is considered a contaminant.
We identified 2007 episodes of bloodstream infections during the 16 year study period and 280 (14%) of these were polymicrobial.
Polymicrobial bloodstream infections were associated with more than 3-fold increase in mortality and an increase in duration of infection.
Gram-negative organisms were second most common (33.3%), followed by fungi (6.1%) and polymicrobial infections (2.6%) (Table 1).

Polymicrobial bloodstream infection was defined as: i) isolation of more than one organism from a single blood culture specimen and ii) isolation of more than one organism in different blood culture specimens during the same bloodstream infectious episode.

Coagulase negative staphylococcal (CONS) infections, skin flora (e.g. Micrococcus spp., Gamma Streptococci) and organisms infrequent in neonates (e.g. Bacillus spp.) were considered real infections when grown from two clinical specimens and a single culture of the above organisms were deemed contaminant and not included in the analyses.

AAP full text (publications.aap.org, including Puopolo 2018) and OUP full text were refused (HTTP 403); those refusals are logged in queries.md and no workaround was used.
Patel2017 percentages are taken from Table 2 because the abstract prints different values.
Reviewer suggestions left unapplied, none blocking: the c16 median of 6.8 days, the c14 Table 3 rows, and the Krasity2024 fetch log, CDC2020 page date and quotes missing from the sheet.
